opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was one of my favorite experiments in the paper, because it moves beyond the classic "evolve a program that solves an optimization problem" setting. Here the thing being evolved is the reasoning pipeline itself: how you orchestrate calls to a language model to solve hard competition math.

The setup was fairly constrained on purpose. We used a relatively small, cheap base model and gave the scaffold a fixed budget of LLM queries per problem. So Shinka couldn't just brute-force its way to a good score by sampling a thousand times and majority voting. It had to figure out how to spend a handful of calls wisely.

A few things stood out to me.

First, what it converged on looked surprisingly human-interpretable. The evolved scaffold roughly does three things. It generates several candidate solutions from different "expert" perspectives. It then has those solutions critically reviewed, almost like peer review where the model checks the reasoning and looks for errors. Finally, it synthesizes the results into a final answer. None of these ingredients are individually new; people have proposed ensembles, self-critique, and debate-style setups before. But Shinka discovered a combination and a particular allocation of the call budget that worked well under the constraint, and it found it fairly sample-efficiently.

Second, there's a real Pareto trade-off between performance and the number of LLM calls, and evolution navigates it in an interesting way. Early in the run you see big jumps from simple structural changes, like adding any form of verification. Later the gains come from much more subtle prompt and orchestration tweaks. That mirrors what we see in other domains: coarse structure first, then refinement.

Third, and this was the part I was most nervous about, the scaffold generalized. We evolved it on one year of AIME problems, and it transferred to held-out years and to different base models, including stronger ones. That suggested we weren't overfitting to quirks of a particular problem set. The scaffold captured something more general about how to structure mathematical reasoning with an LLM.

The bigger lesson for me is that the search space of agent designs is huge, and right now most of it is explored by hand, with researchers writing prompts and pipelines based on intuition. Framing scaffold design as an open-ended program search problem lets you automate a lot of that. And because the output is code, you can read it, understand why it works, and build on it. That interpretability is something you lose if you treat everything as end-to-end training.

There are caveats. The fitness signal on AIME is fairly noisy because there are only so many problems, and you have to be careful about evaluation budgets. But as a proof of concept that Shinka can do meta-level design, evolving the systems that use models rather than just the artifacts they produce, I found it really encouraging.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the first things we tried once ShinkaEvolve was working, and the AIME experiment was kind of a natural fit because you have a very clean, verifiable reward signal — the answer is right or it's wrong — and you have a fixed budget of LLM calls that the scaffold is allowed to use. So the question was: given, say, ten queries to a model, what's the best way to orchestrate those queries to maximize accuracy on competition math?

The thing that surprised me most was how quickly the system rediscovered things that we as a community have spent a lot of time hand-engineering. The seed program was basically a single call, maybe a very simple best-of-n. Within a few dozen generations, Shinka had evolved scaffolds that did things like: generate multiple candidate solutions in parallel, extract the final answers, and then run a sort of critique or verification step where the model is asked to check which of the candidates is actually consistent. And then it layered on majority voting on top of that. So it ended up with a kind of three-stage pipeline — sample, critique, aggregate — that looks a lot like what people have published, but it got there on its own, and crucially it did it with very few samples. We're talking on the order of a hundred-and-fifty-ish program evaluations, not tens of thousands.

And I think that sample efficiency was really the main lesson. It comes from a few design choices in Shinka: we have the parent sampling that balances exploitation of high-performing programs with exploration, we use the novelty rejection based on code embeddings so we don't waste compute re-evaluating near-duplicate scaffolds, and we have an ensemble of LLMs proposing mutations with a bandit that learns which proposer model is actually producing improvements. All of that together meant we could do this kind of search on a laptop-scale compute budget rather than needing a big cluster.

The second thing I learned is a little more sobering, which is that you have to be really careful about what the evolved scaffold is actually optimizing. Because if your validation set is small, and AIME is small — it's like thirty problems per year — the evolutionary process will happily find things that are specific to those thirty problems. So we had to hold out a separate set to check that the gains transferred. And they did transfer reasonably well, including across different underlying LLMs, which was nice, because it suggested the scaffold was capturing something general about how to structure reasoning and verification rather than just memorizing quirks of a particular model.

And then the third thing, which I find genuinely interesting, is the interpretability angle. Because the output of this process is code, not weights, you can actually read what it came up with. You can see the prompts it wrote for the critique step, you can see how it decided to allocate the query budget — like, it would sometimes spend more calls on verification than on generation, which is not what I would have guessed. So it's a bit like having a research assistant that runs a lot of small experiments and leaves you a legible trail of what worked.

The caveat I'd give is that these are relatively simple scaffolds. We're not evolving something as complex as a full agent framework with tool use and memory. But the fact that even in this constrained setting you get nontrivial discoveries with so little compute makes me pretty optimistic about scaling it up.

astra-6.text:
The interesting question is how much of an agent’s performance comes from the model and how much comes from the scaffold around it. For mathematics, that scaffold determines whether the model revisits an assumption, checks a candidate answer, or spends its remaining budget exploring another approach.

I’d be careful, though, about equating a higher AIME score with discovering a generally better reasoning agent. You’re optimizing against a particular evaluation, and you can end up selecting something that works well on those problems without transferring elsewhere. You also have to separate improvements in how computation is allocated from improvements that simply use more computation.

So the lesson I’d emphasize is methodological: evolve the scaffold, but test it on held-out problems under comparable budgets. Then inspect what changed. Did the search discover a useful verification step? Did it eliminate unnecessary work? That’s what makes the result informative beyond the score itself.

sol-6.1.text:
The main lesson was that the scaffold around the model is itself something you can optimize. You’re not just searching for a better prompt; you’re searching over how the agent spends its compute, checks its work, and combines candidate solutions.

For AIME, that makes the evaluation especially important. If you let the scaffold use more model calls, you need to distinguish an improvement in the strategy from an improvement that simply comes from spending more compute. And if you repeatedly optimize against a small set of problems, you need held-out problems to see whether the strategy generalizes.

So I’d frame the takeaway as moving from hand-designing an agent loop to treating that loop as a program you can evolve. The interesting question then becomes: what structure does evolution discover that we wouldn’t have thought to write ourselves?
